doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

title: How head arrangements work
summary: Foster explains riffs passing between sections and how each player finds his part without written music.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Can you give our future viewers an idea of what a head arrangement was like? I mean how that kind of thing happened?

Well a head arrangement probably started with one idea or motif if you will, that was expressed by one of the other sections, maybe the saxophones. Like for instance “Jumpin’ At the Woodside.” [scats] And the brass sort of punctuated the licks that came out of the saxophone section. [scats] And they interwove these things and, any section could be the source of one of these riffs or licks that was the main melodic statement of the song, and everybody else just knew how to fall in line and do something to enhance that melody.
And were some of those arrangements done without being written out?
Oh, totally without being written out. Definitely.
That’s a concept that’s kind of lost now.

Every now and then you go, we go to play behind a singer or something, and we’ll have to do what they call “set riffs.” You know, you set a riff, which behind the blues is fairly simple because one guy just picks up his horn and he does something and it sounds pretty good and everybody just joins in on that. Now to emphasize the thing most times you do it in unison to start with, and then about the third or fourth chorus, guys go into a little harmonic thing on it.
And you just know what, you just know how to catch your pitch off of that.
Oh yeah. Oh definitely. You know exactly what —
Everybody can figure out what part he’s to play, depending on the position in the section, in the orchestra.
So if you hear the lead alto do something and you’re the second alto, you’re gonna play about a third below that?
Yeah, you play a third below that. You know you’re going to be under him. You never go over.

The first tenor or second or third under that, the second tenor, the second or third and the baritone can either double what the first alto has done, or pick some low tonic, low root sounds, that give it that heavy sound. The same thing happens in the trumpets and trombone sections.
You know but that to me it seems like it would make for exciting music where the players themselves don’t know everything that’s going to happen when the tune starts.
It has been known to build into some exciting moments, yeah. No doubt about that.
It’s a great feeling when that happens. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
